stem:
What will this Python code print?

print('Hello, World!')
explanation_after: print() is Python's way of outputting text. The text inside the quotes is displayed exactly as written. This is traditionally the first program every programmer writes.

stem: Which of these is valid Python code?
explanation_after: Python is case-sensitive (print not PRINT). Strings must be in quotes. print(hello) would look for a variable called hello, not the text 'hello'.

stem: Why is Python particularly popular for AI and machine learning?

options.text: It was invented specifically for AI
It has a vast ecosystem of ML libraries and readable syntax
AI can only be coded in Python

explanation_after: Python's readable syntax lowers the barrier to entry. Its ecosystem — NumPy, PyTorch, TensorFlow, scikit-learn, Hugging Face — is unmatched. Speed-critical parts are written in C/C++ underneath.

stem: Which Python line correctly prints the text YourName?
explanation_after: In Python, text (strings) must be wrapped in quotes — either single 'like this' or double "like this". Without quotes, Python treats it as a variable name.

stem:
What does this code print?

print('Value:', 5 + 3)
explanation_after: print() can take multiple comma-separated arguments and automatically inserts a space between them. Python first evaluates 5 + 3 to get 8, then prints the text 'Value:' followed by a space and 8, giving 'Value: 8'.

stem: NumPy and PyTorch are Python libraries, yet they perform millions of numeric computations very quickly. How is this possible if Python itself is a relatively slow, interpreted language?

options.text: Python secretly compiles itself into machine code at runtime for every program
These libraries implement their core numeric operations in fast compiled languages like C, C++, or CUDA, and Python code simply calls into that fast compiled code
They avoid using the Python interpreter entirely, even to write the surrounding code
They only work on supercomputers, never on ordinary laptops

explanation_after: This is the real reason Python dominates ML despite being 'slow': the heavy numeric lifting happens in optimized, compiled C/C++/CUDA code underneath, while Python provides the easy-to-read layer on top that calls into it. You write readable Python; the actual matrix multiplications run in fast, low-level code.
